notes: PASSES BY 0.45. 78/0.30 + 84/0.25 + 77/0.25 + 84/0.20 = 80.45 against a threshold of 80. Read that as a pass on arithmetic, not on merit. The two cheapest fixes below (chunk 44 and chunk 24) are single-clause edits and would move this to a comfortable pass; do not take the green light as a reason to skip them. What this script does exceptionally well, and what a human should weigh before opening the lock: every one of research.md's named traps is handled correctly. The per-transit water figure is spoken as an estimate and never as fact; 'Panamax' never appears where a Neopanamax bid is being priced; the El Nino/climate-projection conflation that research called 'the single easiest way for the critic to fail factual fidelity' is separated explicitly across chunks 47-50; the marginal-nine-percent caveat survives to chunk 61; the household ratio is 'roughly a hundred times' and never a decimal. The '7% less water', the '60% basin recovery' and the 36.60 m beam - all three on research's do-not-put-on-screen list - appear nowhere. That is genuine discipline and it is the reason this is an 80 and not a 62.

FACTUAL - chunk 44. 'The 2024 financial year closed twenty-one percent below the one before it' cites s5, whose twenty-one percent is 9,944 deep-draft TRANSITS against FY2023 - not revenue, not profit, not the financial result the sentence's wording promises. A viewer hears money. Research section 5.1 also records three competing FY2024 counts (9,944 deep-draft in s5, 11,240 all-craft in s4, 9,936 in trade press) and asks the script to name the basis it picks and hold it; this sentence names none. Fix: 'Deep-draft transits in financial year 2024 came in twenty-one percent below the year before.' Two words of basis and the number becomes true. This is the highest-value single edit in the script.

FACTUAL - chunk 24. 'Three separate outlets confirm the figure' cites s16 alone. s16's supports field records ONE independent confirmation of the $5.3m and names the $4.6m predecessor; it cannot carry a claim about three outlets. The claim is true of the source set (s15, s16, s19 all have it) but not of the source cited, which is precisely the failure nothing downstream catches. Fix: cite all three, or better, cut the line. It is sourcing chatter in the voiceover, it belongs in the description, and it costs 2.4 seconds inside b3, the fastest beat in the episode.

PACING - chunks 35-36. Fifteen point two seconds of pure methodology, sitting between the '$5.3 million buys what?' question and the drinking-water reveal: 'The Authority publishes its water in millions of cubic metres a day, not gallons per ship' plus 'No primary document of theirs states a per-transit figure, so hold that number as a band, not a measurement.' No new information, no escalation, no image - a dead stretch by the fifteen-second rule, at the worst possible position, right as b4 is trying to accelerate. 'Hold that number as a band' also addresses the viewer as a producer rather than a narrator. Fix: keep one spoken clause - 'and that is an estimate, not a measurement' - and put the rest on the chart as a caption reading 'approx. 200,000 m3, plus or minus 10 percent, est. - ACP publishes hm3/day, not per-transit'. Recovers about twelve seconds and the honesty ends up where it is actually more visible, not less.

FACTUAL - chunk 38. 'Gatun Lake is the drinking water for fifty-five percent of Panama's population' cites s7, which says the canal WATERSHED supplies 55 percent; s5 makes clear that is Gatun and Alhajuela together, and s6 frames the same fact a third way as 80 percent of consumption in three provinces. The script narrows a two-lake watershed to one lake, and it does it on the line the entire moral weight of the episode rests on - the line chunk 39 answers with 'The same lake.' Fix: 'The canal's watershed is the drinking water for fifty-five percent of Panama's population.' Identical force, and it is what the source says. Keep 'The same lake' - the transit water does come from Gatun; it is the 55 percent that belongs to the watershed.

FACTUAL - chunk 56. 'The canal's own average lands near two dollars thirteen a cubic metre' - three significant figures, stated to the cent, derived from a divisor the script itself called an estimate twenty seconds earlier. Research puts a plus-or-minus-ten-percent band on the 200,000 m3 figure, which puts the canal's average anywhere between $1.94 and $2.37, and the $27 between $24 and $30. Chunk 58 gets this right by saying 'about twenty-seven'; chunk 56 does not. This is an estimate presented as a measurement, which the rubric names explicitly. Fix: 'lands near two dollars a cubic metre' and let the chart carry the band. The middle bar is the episode's most original number - it is worth stating at the precision it actually has.

PACING - chunks 7-9. The promise beat spends sixteen seconds naming three prices and attaching a number to none of them: 'What a household in Panama City paid for it. What the canal earns on it on an average day.' That is a contents page read aloud, and it lands exactly where the cold open's momentum has to be spent rather than banked. Fix: attach the cheapest number to the first item - 'Twenty-one cents, for a household in Panama City' - so the viewer leaves the promise holding one real figure and a visible gap, instead of three empty slots. Costs nothing in length and converts a dead stretch into a hook.

PACING - chunks 66-69. The surcharge ladder speaks four lake-level/percentage pairs (84.3 to 2, 82 to 5, just-over-79 to nearly 9, plus $10,000 over 300 feet) in about twenty-four seconds, over a chart that already displays all four. b5 carries roughly twenty distinct numbers in 117 seconds - one every six seconds - and this is the stretch where the fact rate stops landing, the rubric's opposite failure. Fix: speak one point only, 82 feet and five percent, because that is the number the cold open promised and the thumbnail sells; let the curve animate the other three; and hold the flat $10,000 for the final line of the beat so it lands as the fee no ship escapes rather than as the fourth item in a list.

FACTUAL - chunks 75 and 77. The episode's closing question rests on 'a strait that never actually closed' and asks how it set the price of Panamanian water. No source in the pack covers that strait, that conflict, or the causal link between either and the auction price. s17 supports only that the Administrator dates the old $135,000 price to before a conflict - that is his dating, not a demonstrated cause. The loop is the one place the script asserts a causal claim it cannot cite, and it is the last thing the viewer hears. Fix: either add the source before LOCK 1, or put the claim back in the Administrator's mouth where it is sourced: 'The man who runs the canal dates the old price to a war twelve thousand kilometres away. Episode two asks why that moved Panamanian water.' Same tease, no unattributed cause.

FACTUAL - chunk 47. 'The Authority attributes this year to a forecast El Nino, which is weather' cites s2, whose recorded supports field covers the 34-percent rainfall and 44-percent inflow shortfalls and the postponed draft increases, and says nothing about El Nino. Research section 5.6 does attribute the El Nino framing to the ACP and to s2, so this is most likely a source record whose supports field is short rather than a wrong claim - but as the pack stands today the citation does not carry the sentence, and the sentence is load-bearing: it is half of the weather-versus-climate separation that chunks 48-50 build on. Fix: extend s2's supports in sources.json to record the El Nino attribution, or move the citation to whichever source actually carries it. Resolve before LOCK 1, not after.

SENSITIVITY - chunk 63 and the clippable flag on b5. The line that will actually get clipped from this episode is 'roughly a hundred times what the household paid', and it is the one line in the script that is misleading without the sentence that precedes it. The script gets the order right for a linear viewer - the scarcity-signal caveat is chunk 62, the ratio is chunk 63 - and then marks b5 clippable, handing a short-form cut that drops the caveat and keeps the outrage. Fix: fold the qualifier into the clippable line itself - 'roughly a hundred times what a household paid, for the three slots a day that go to auction' - so it survives being cut out of context. Six extra words, and the vertical stops being a claim the research explicitly calls wrong.

SENSITIVITY / WHAT SEPARATES THIS FROM A 95. The pack sets reverence_required false and bans no depictions, so no rule here is broken - this is a framing note, not a violation. The episode prices a country's drinking water at a hundred times what its people pay for it, and never spends a beat on who carries that. 'The same lake.' at chunk 39 is the best sentence in the script and it is followed immediately by hydrology; chunk 63 delivers the hundred-times ratio and moves straight to the tariff ladder. Meanwhile research recorded 38 farming communities and about 2,000 residents facing displacement for the reservoir meant to fix this (s20), and a live Escazu Agreement dispute, and this script does not know they exist. Nothing in it is wrong. But a data explainer that treats a nation's water supply purely as a pricing curiosity is a thinner thing than this research supports. One sentence of human consequence after chunk 63 would cost four seconds. Related and smaller: chunk 29's 'and the answer is flat' characterises a living named official's delivery in a way no source records - either cut 'flat' or source it.

HOOK - chunks 1-2, and why this is an 84 rather than a 94. The open clears every trap the rubric names: no bumper, no definition, no welcome, and the question in sentence two is genuinely one a stranger cannot answer. A formula on frame one that turns lake depth into money is the freshest cold open available from this research and it is correctly chosen. Two things hold it back. First, chunk 2 is a two-part question - 'Who writes something like that, and what happens when the lake falls?' - and the halves compete; 'who writes something like that' is the weaker one and it goes first. Cut it and the remaining question hits alone. Second, no stake is named for the first eleven seconds: 'into money' is abstract, and Panama is not spoken until chunk 3. Consider seeding scale into sentence one - 'There is a formula that turns the depth of a Panamanian lake into money, and last month it helped price one ship's crossing at five point three million dollars' is one sentence and it buys the next thirty seconds outright without spoiling b3, which still owns the whole series.

MINOR, batched, all one-word fixes: chunk 15's 'anyone can bid' is not in s1, which records the slot counts and the auction share but nothing about eligibility - drop the clause or source it. Chunk 43 says 'from a normal thirty-four' where s13 says 34 to 36, and the beat sheet for b4 already says 34 to 36 - match the source. Chunk 60's 'thirty-four daily slots' omits s1's fall to 32 from 15 September, a date the episode's own 1 September framing has nearly reached; 'thirty-four daily slots, and falling to thirty-two this month' costs four words and pre-empts a correction in the comments. Chunk 21 cites s15 for 'northbound', which only s19 records - s15 carries everything else in that sentence, so add s19 or drop the direction. Chunk 34 says 'hold that number as a band' but never states the band's width anywhere in the script - if the caption fix in the chunks 35-36 note is taken, this resolves itself.

STRUCTURAL, for the record and not against the score: beat conformance is good and worth keeping. Actual runtimes against targets are b1 33s/30, b2 37.5s/35, b3 104.5s/110, b4 103.4s/95, b5 116.6s/115, b6 36.9s/35 - total about 432 seconds including 46.6 seconds of pause, which lands at 7.2 minutes inside the format's 6-8. Only b4 is meaningfully over, by nine percent, and the chunks 35-36 cut fixes that on its own. Pause placement is the quiet strength here: the 1000-1200ms holds after chunks 6, 21, 38, 58 and 77 all sit under the episode's five biggest reveals, and the short punch lines around the record bid ('Not for the cargo.' 'For the crossing.') give the densest beat its only room to breathe. Whatever else changes, do not compress those.
